text: An Azure Network Security Group and an AWS Security Group solve the exact same problem — deciding which traffic gets to a resource — but they're built on genuinely different models, and mixing them up is a real source of misconfigured rules. This lesson walks both syntaxes side by side, plus the AWS construct people usually forget about until they need an explicit Deny.

An NSG rule has a priority from 100 to 4096, a direction, an access value of Allow or Deny, a protocol, and address and port ranges. Azure walks the rules in priority order — lower number first — and stops at the first match. Every NSG also ships with default rules you can't delete, sitting at 65000 and above, so your own rules always win. NSGs are stateful: an inbound Allow automatically permits the matching response traffic back out. They can attach at the subnet and the NIC, and Azure checks both.

A Security Group rule has no priority field at all, because a Security Group can only ever Allow — there's no Deny action. Every SG starts from an implicit deny-all, and when several groups attach to the same network interface, their rules are simply unioned together; there's nothing to shadow, so order never matters. SGs are stateful too. The AWS-only trick worth knowing: a rule's source can be another security group's ID instead of an IP range, so membership tracks autoscaled instances automatically — Azure's closest equivalent is an Application Security Group.

If a design genuinely needs an explicit Deny in AWS, that's not a Security Group's job — it's a Network ACL. A NACL attaches to a subnet, is evaluated in numbered rule order with first match winning, just like NSG priority, and supports both Allow and Deny. The catch is that NACLs are stateless, so inbound and outbound each need their own explicit rule; nothing comes back automatically.

Lay the three side by side and the picture clicks: NSGs attach to a subnet or a NIC and support Deny; Security Groups attach only to the instance's network interface and only support Allow, unioned across every group attached; NACLs attach to the subnet, support Deny, and are stateless where the other two are stateful. Knowing which one you're actually editing is half the job of debugging a blocked connection in either cloud.

With per-resource filtering covered, the next lesson moves up a layer: Azure Firewall and AWS Network Firewall, the managed appliances that sit in front of an entire network rather than a single subnet or instance, and how their rule models compare.
